title: The autonomy paradox: junior developers report feeling more capable and less like the author of their own work
summary: A qualitative study of thirteen interns and junior developers finds that what decides whether a newcomer uses AI or works by hand is neither deadline nor task difficulty but whether they can check the result — the authors call this 'verification-conditioned use'. Two findings bear directly on how the work is experienced. The first is an autonomy paradox: participants describe feeling more capable while feeling less ownership of what they produce. The second is a first-person denial of dependence — newcomers readily identify AI dependence in peers while rejecting it in themselves, a gap between actual reliance and self-perception. The authors join these into a 'formative paradox': the shallow learning AI induces makes it harder to build the critical-judgment competence that participants say the market has begun to demand of them. What participants themselves report makes their AI use sustainable is a set of personal disciplines — reviewing before accepting, refusing to use output they do not understand, asking the tool for explanations, and keeping deliberate practice outside AI-assisted work.
whyItMatters: Ownership is usually managed as an org-design property — who is on the rota, whose name is on the service. This finds it eroding at the level of felt authorship even where formal ownership is unchanged, which no team-structure change will fix.

The denial-of-dependence finding means self-report is an unreliable instrument here. Leaders asking juniors whether they rely on AI too much will get a systematically reassuring answer, including from those most affected.

The disciplines participants credit for sustainable use — reviewing before accepting, refusing output they do not understand, practising outside AI-assisted work — are currently individual coping strategies carried by the least senior people. Whether they become team norms is a leadership choice.
recommendedActions: Measure junior competence through work that cannot be verification-conditioned — unassisted debugging, design reasoning, code explanation — rather than through throughput or self-assessment.
Make 'refuse output you do not understand' an explicit, protected team norm rather than a personal discipline, so that acting on it does not read as being slow.
risksAndCaveats: Thirteen participants, qualitative and self-reported, single study, not replicated. The interview window is not stated in the abstract, so how current the accounts are cannot be established from the source.
Participants who volunteer for interviews about AI and their careers are plausibly those with the strongest feelings about it; the sample is not a cross-section of junior developers.

The study spans learning, autonomy and market entry. Its learning and hiring findings belong to other sectors; only the autonomy, ownership and self-perception themes are the basis for surfacing it here.
